short: The G7 Hiroshima AI Process produced two documents in October 2023: International Guiding Principles and an International Code of Conduct for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems. The code lists eleven actions, is voluntary, and since 2025 has an OECD reporting framework where companies publish how they follow it.
title: G7 Hiroshima AI Process Code of Conduct
subtitle: The 2023 G7 guiding principles and code of conduct for organizations developing advanced AI
body_html:
What the Hiroshima process is

The Hiroshima AI Process was launched by the G7 under Japan's 2023 presidency to agree a common approach to advanced AI, meaning frontier foundation models and generative systems. On October 30, 2023, the G7 leaders issued two documents: the International Guiding Principles for Organizations Developing Advanced AI Systems, and the International Code of Conduct, which turns the principles into actions for developers. Both are voluntary.

In May 2024 Japan launched the Hiroshima AI Process Friends Group, a voluntary group of countries that support the process; it started with 49 members, including the G7, and passed 55 by 2025. On February 7, 2025 the OECD opened the Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework, under which companies publish a standard report on how they follow the code; the first 19 reports were published in April 2025 and the first round closed at 25.

The eleven actions

  1. Take appropriate measures throughout development to identify, evaluate and mitigate risks, including red-teaming and testing.
  2. Identify and mitigate vulnerabilities, incidents and patterns of misuse after deployment.
  3. Publicly report advanced AI systems' capabilities, limitations and domains of appropriate and inappropriate use.
  4. Work toward responsible information sharing and reporting of incidents among organizations.
  5. Develop, implement and disclose AI governance and risk management policies.
  6. Invest in security controls, including physical, cyber and insider threat safeguards.
  7. Develop and deploy content authentication and provenance mechanisms such as watermarking.
  8. Prioritize research on societal, safety and security risks.
  9. Prioritize development of AI systems that address the world's greatest challenges.
  10. Advance international technical standards.
  11. Implement data input measures and protections for personal data and intellectual property.

How conformity is shown

Through the OECD reporting framework. A company submits a report against the eleven actions and the OECD publishes it. There is no audit and no sanction; the discipline is that the reports are public and comparable.

Why it matters

The code is the closest thing to a global baseline for frontier model developers that the major developers have all accepted. Its actions reappear in the EU AI Act's general-purpose AI obligations and in the GPAI Code of Practice, and the reporting framework is where a reader can see what a developer says it does.

Related instruments

The OECD AI Principles are the foundation it cites. The EU AI Act general-purpose AI chapter is the binding counterpart in Europe. See the Standards and Frameworks hub.

Primary sources

  • Japan Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Hiroshima AI Process, principles and code of conduct texts
  • OECD.AI, Hiroshima AI Process Reporting Framework, published company reports
